question: A SQL Server 2025 worker reads document revision 41, generates its embedding outside the write transaction, then runs the shown update. Revision 42 has meanwhile committed; the stored embedding still represents revision 40. SourceRevision is an application-maintained number that changes with the text. Which additional predicate rejects this stale write so the worker can reread and regenerate?

answerChoices.text: AND SourceRevision >= @revision
AND EmbeddingRevision < @revision
AND SourceRevision = @revision
AND Embedding IS NOT NULL

explanation: Require the current source revision to equal the revision used to generate the proposed embedding.
deepExplanation: A changed-row notification is not a guarantee that asynchronous work is still current when it finishes. Here 42 does not equal 41, so the guarded update affects no row and the worker can retry from current text. Comparing only the old embedding revision accepts a newer-than-old but still obsolete result. This is a persistence guard, not a complete exactly-once consumer.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: Revision 42 satisfies >= 41, so this admits the stale revision-41 vector.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: The old embedding revision is 40, so 40 < 41 also admits a vector that is behind the current text.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: An existing embedding says nothing about whether the completed work represents the current source revision.

question: On SQL Server 2025 at compatibility level 170, documents have unique DocumentId values and each produces multiple chunks. Model access, chunk input limits and destination vector width are validated. The empty destination must receive one row per source document/chunk, with the embedding generated from that row's ChunkText. Which repair fixes both defects in the shown insertion?

answerChoices.text: Join Chunks to Documents on DocumentId, but continue embedding d.Body.
Keep the CROSS JOIN, but pass c.chunk to AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS.
Select DISTINCT over the current CROSS JOIN, retaining the existing embedding input.
Join on DocumentId and pass c.chunk to AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS.

explanation: Correlate each chunk with its own document and generate the vector from the chunk text being stored.
deepExplanation: The CTE already produces the correct document/chunk relationship through CROSS APPLY. The later CROSS JOIN destroys that relationship by pairing every document with every chunk. Independently, embedding d.Body represents the entire document rather than c.chunk. Fixing only one defect leaves either incorrect ownership or a text/vector mismatch.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: It repairs ownership but still generates whole-document vectors for rows labeled with individual chunks.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: It repairs the embedding input but still associates each chunk with unrelated DocumentId values.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: DISTINCT does not restore the missing document relationship or change what text is embedded.

subskill: Design and implement chunks for embeddings
codeSnippet:
WITH Chunks AS (
    SELECT d.DocumentId, c.chunk_order, c.chunk
    FROM dbo.Documents AS d
    CROSS APPLY AI_GENERATE_CHUNKS(
        SOURCE = d.Body, CHUNK_TYPE = FIXED, CHUNK_SIZE = 600
    ) AS c
)
INSERT dbo.ChunkVectors(DocumentId, ChunkOrder, ChunkText, Embedding)
SELECT d.DocumentId, c.chunk_order, c.chunk,
       AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(d.Body USE MODEL SupportEmbedding)
FROM dbo.Documents AS d
CROSS JOIN Chunks AS c;

question: A multilingual handbook uses fixed character chunks before embedding. Tests find some 400-character chunks contain 620 model tokens, exceeding the stipulated 512-token limit. Other chunks separate a restriction from the sentence it qualifies. Which revised preparation policy addresses both observed failures without assuming a fixed characters-to-tokens ratio?

answerChoices.text: Use 512 characters for every chunk and keep the existing boundaries.
Validate token counts for the chosen model and use context-preserving boundaries or overlap within the limit.
Keep the oversized chunks but normalize each generated vector to unit length.
Split each document into single words without retaining neighboring context.

explanation: Check actual model-token counts while preserving enough neighboring text to retain the qualifying context.
deepExplanation: Input-size compliance and semantic completeness are different design requirements. A character limit cannot be assumed to enforce the measured token limit, while extremely small chunks can lose meaning. Boundary and overlap choices must be evaluated on this corpus rather than treated as universally optimal numbers.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: The measured character/token mismatch already disproves a one-to-one size rule.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: Post-generation vector scaling does not repair an oversized model input or missing source context.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: Short units may fit the limit but discard the neighboring qualification that the tests require.

question: A SQL Server 2025 search application will replace embedding model A with model B. Both return 1,536 components, but the supplied model contracts say their coordinates are not interchangeable. Queries must cover the entire corpus throughout backfill. Which rollout preserves meaningful comparisons while moving to B?

answerChoices.text: Keep A queries on A vectors; build a separate complete B-vector snapshot, validate it, then switch query encoding and storage together.
Encode queries with B immediately and compare them with the remaining A vectors because their dimensions match.
Normalize A vectors and compare them with B queries without regenerating the corpus.
Replace A vectors in place and search only the rows already converted to B during backfill.

explanation: Maintain a matched encoder/vector snapshot until the replacement corpus is complete and validated, then switch them together.
deepExplanation: Vector width is a storage contract, not a model-space compatibility guarantee. The query-pattern training uses the same model for query and stored vectors. A separate replacement snapshot avoids mixing spaces and preserves full-corpus coverage while backfill runs; it requires extra storage and explicit routing rather than promising a free migration.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Equal component counts do not override the stated incompatibility of the two coordinate systems.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: Normalization changes scale, not the supplied models' incompatible semantic coordinate systems.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: It avoids comparing A with B only by dropping the not-yet-converted part of the required searchable corpus.
